statement: In adults who drink, whether any remedy or way of coping reduces anxiety or low mood during a hangover was not tested in any of the 22 studies of a systematic review, which included no intervention study, and its authors call for one (Rothman et al., 2026). In three interview studies (109 young adults, mostly students, in Norway and the United Kingdom), people said that sharing the hangover with friends who had also been drinking eased their distress, which they traced mainly to regret about what they had done while drunk, gaps in memory and a wasted day; in one cross-sectional survey, people with more resilience reported less severe hangovers and people who used avoidant coping reported more severe ones. Evidence is insufficient to say whether any strategy changes how people feel during a hangover. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Nobody has tested anything that eases the worry or low mood of a hangover; in interviews, young people said that talking it over with friends helped.
population: Adults who drink: three interview studies of young adults, mostly students (66, 23 and 20 participants), and one cross-sectional survey of 648 respondents (described inconsistently in the review), within a systematic review
exposure: Ways of coping with a hangover: sharing it with friends (as described in interviews); resilience and coping style (measured in one survey)
comparator: No comparison group: interview accounts, and correlations across survey respondents
outcome: Anxiety, low mood, guilt and other distress during a hangover; hangover severity
magnitude: No intervention tested. Interview themes in all three studies: distress linked to behaviour while drunk, memory gaps and a wasted day; sharing the experience with friends eased it. One survey: resilience correlated with less severe and avoidant coping with more severe hangovers (coefficients not given in the review).

evidence.extracted: Across the three interview studies, people described sadness, guilt, regret, shame, worry and embarrassment during hangovers, prompted mostly by behaviour while drunk that clashed with their beliefs, catastrophic thinking and a sense of a wasted day; they said that bonding with friends and sharing the unpleasantness of the hangover helped ease these feelings.

evidence.extracted: In one cross-sectional survey, depression, anxiety, stress and avoidant coping correlated positively, and mental resilience negatively, with hangover severity; the review gives no coefficients.

risk_of_bias.note: Interview accounts and a single cross-sectional correlation, with no comparison group.

indirectness.note: The evidence describes what people say helps and which traits go with milder hangovers, not the effect of doing anything.

imprecision.note: Not applicable to themes; no estimates.

grade.reasoning: Observational and qualitative evidence starts low; downgraded for risk of bias and indirectness, giving very low. Status single study: the claim rests on one review; its interview theme recurs in three studies and its coping association comes from one survey. A remedy that was never tested is itself the finding here (decision p-day-after).
